title: Academic writing: text structure
subtitle: reiterate, epitomise, subsume, beyond the scope of
summary: Structure an essay in academic English - reiterate, expound, posit, account for - and signpost your argument from prefacing it to being forced to conclude.

lesson.heading: Explaining, reinforcing, exemplifying
rows: reiterate
repeat, restate
The Prime Minister reiterated her concern that the debate should not be dominated by personal attacks.
summarise
describe briefly the main facts or ideas
She summarised the new policy as being progressive and radical.
epitomise
be a perfect example of
Peter Burnett's comments epitomise the attitude of many parents nowadays.
assert
say that something is certainly true
He asserted that schools are to blame for anti-social behaviour among children.
expound
develop, propose
It was a philosophy first expounded by John Ruskin in the 19th century.
underscore
emphasise
The recent events underscore the need for a better understanding of the environmental impact of biotechnology.
posit
suggest as a basic fact or principle
Several scientists have posited a link between climate change and bird migration patterns.
account for
explain, find the cause of
In an attempt to account for the lack of interest, political analysts have looked at past voting patterns.

lesson.heading: Categorising and including
lesson.text: **Comprise** and **make up** both mean consist of; something can also **be comprised of** its parts. To **subsume** things under a heading is to bring them together under it, and a book that **embraces** a number of issues covers or includes them.

examples.text: Chinese visitors **comprised** / **made up** 70% of the hotel's guests last year.
The course **is comprised of** two elements: reading and writing.
These two approaches can be **subsumed under** one heading.
The book **embraces** a number of issues, from economic to religious ones.

examples.note: = label as belonging to a particular type or class

lesson.heading: Consist of
lesson.text: **Consist** is followed by **of** when we refer to the elements that compose something. This is a very common mistake in academic writing.

examples.text: The country **consists of** five major regions.
The course **consists of** five modules, from which students must choose three.

lesson.heading: Structuring the text: beginning, connecting and focusing
rows: mapping out the text at the beginning
I should like to preface my argument with a true story.
connecting points
I shall return to this point later in my essay.
focusing
This brings me/us to my next area of discussion, which is finance.
focusing on a new question
I should now like to address the question of the arms race.
ordering points
The arguments are presented in ascending/descending order of importance.
lesson.note: In ascending order means least important first; in descending order means most important first.

lesson.heading: Structuring the text: referring, limiting and concluding
rows: quoting or referring
The ideas of several writers will be cited in support of the argument.
referring indirectly
The text alludes to several themes that need closer examination.
including material only briefly
There will only be space to touch upon the big question of political responsibility.
excluding material
It is impossible to deal with all the issues in this short essay.
excluding a whole topic
Discussion of the roots of the problem is beyond the scope of this essay.
drawing conclusions
We are forced to conclude that unemployment will always be with us.
lesson.note: To touch upon something is to include it only briefly; to deal with something is to give all the necessary information about it.

lesson.text: Underscore, reiterate and posit are the essay-writing versions of emphasise, repeat and suggest - use them when the register needs to lift.

exercises.prompt: Make it more formal: The response from the public ___ the importance of having a full investigation of the facts.
exercises.explanation: To underscore something is to emphasise it.

exercises.prompt: Make it more formal: This view of the world was originally ___ by the Ancient Greek philosophers.
exercises.explanation: To expound an idea is to develop or propose it.

exercises.prompt: Make it more formal: It is not easy to ___ the fall in population of these birds.
exercises.hint: (two words: explain, find the cause of)
exercises.explanation: To account for something is to explain it or find its cause.

exercises.prompt: Make it more formal: Economists have ___ a link between exchange rates and a general lack of confidence in the European Union.
exercises.explanation: To posit something is to suggest it as a basic fact or principle.

exercises.prompt: Make it more formal: I should like to ___ here that the issue is not one that can be easily resolved.
exercises.explanation: To reiterate is to repeat or restate.

exercises.prompt: Make it more formal: The recent events ___ the dilemma faced by politicians the world over.
exercises.hint: (formal verb for 'are the best example of')
exercises.explanation: If something epitomises a situation, it is a perfect example of it.

exercises.prompt: Make it more formal: In a 2010 article, Charles Plestow ___ that the whole European Medieval era had been misinterpreted.
exercises.explanation: To assert something is to say that it is certainly true.

exercises.prompt: Make it more formal: The lecturer ___ the main arguments of her talk at the end.
exercises.explanation: To summarise is to describe briefly the main facts or ideas.

exercises.prompt: Which rewrite of '70% of the landmass is mountain ranges' uses comprise correctly?
options: Mountain ranges comprise 70% of the landmass.
Mountain ranges comprise of 70% of the landmass.
70% of the landmass comprises in mountain ranges.
Mountain ranges are comprising 70% of the landmass.
exercises.explanation: Comprise means consist of, so no preposition follows it; you can also say the landmass is comprised of mountain ranges.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite with consist: The course ___ five modules, from which students must choose three.
exercises.explanation: Consist is always followed by of when referring to the elements that compose something.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite with subsume: I think these three sections can all be ___ one heading.
exercises.explanation: To subsume things under a heading is to bring them together under it.

exercises.prompt: I shall ___ to this line of argument later in the book.
exercises.explanation: I shall return to this point later is a standard way of connecting points in an essay.

exercises.prompt: The question of monetary union ___ us to our next topic: the idea of a federal Europe.
exercises.explanation: This brings me/us to my next area of discussion is a standard focusing phrase.

exercises.prompt: Smithies just ___ upon the subject of internet policing, but does not go into it in depth.
exercises.explanation: To touch upon something is to include it only briefly.

exercises.prompt: I shall attempt to ___ the problem of censorship later in this discussion.
exercises.explanation: I should now like to address the question of ... is a standard focusing phrase.

exercises.prompt: Psychological factors in learning foreign languages are ___ this article.
exercises.explanation: If something is beyond the scope of an essay, it is outside its topic area.

exercises.prompt: I shall discuss the poets in ___ order, that is to say I shall comment on the least important ones first.
exercises.explanation: Ascending order puts the least important first; descending order does the opposite.

exercises.prompt: In the final analysis, we are ___ that there is little hope of stamping out illegal drugs altogether.
exercises.hint: (three words: have no choice but to believe)
exercises.explanation: We are forced to conclude that ... is a standard way of drawing conclusions.

exercises.prompt: Match each essay phrase with the job it does in the text.

pairs.left: I should like to preface my argument with ...
pairs.right: mapping out the text at the beginning

pairs.left: The ideas of several writers will be cited ...
The text alludes to several themes ...
It is impossible to deal with all the issues ...
We are forced to conclude that ...

exercises.statement: If a writer only touches upon a subject, they discuss it in considerable depth.
exercises.explanation: The opposite - to touch upon something is to include it only briefly.

exercises.prompt: Does each verb reinforce a point, or organise the text?
